## Problem 1 – Insurance Claims

### Part A: 95% CI for Proportion with Exaggerated Loss

```{r}
urlRemote <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
pathGithub <- "EricBrownTTU/ISQS5346/main/"
filename <- "InsuranceClaims.csv"
InsuranceClaims <- read.csv(paste0(urlRemote, pathGithub, filename))
n <- nrow(InsuranceClaims)
x <- sum(InsuranceClaims$Buildup == 1)
p_hat <- x / n
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
lower <- p_hat - z * se
upper <- p_hat + z * se
c(lower, upper)
```

**Explanation**
This confidence interval estimates the proportion of claims with exaggerated loss. It uses the normal approximation to the binomial.

### Part B: 95% CI for Mean Excess Payment
```{r}
excess <- InsuranceClaims$ExcessPayment
mean_excess <- mean(excess)
sd_excess <- sd(excess)
n_excess <- length(excess)
se_excess <- sd_excess / sqrt(n_excess)
t <- qt(1-(0.05/2), df = n_excess - 1)
ci_excess <- c(mean_excess - t * se_excess, mean_excess + t * se_excess)
ci_excess
```
**Explanation**
This confidence interval gives the estimated range for the average excess payment using the t-distribution.

### Part C: Company Estimates Check
```{r}
is_in_prop_ci <- 0.75 >= lower & 0.75 <= upper
is_in_excess_ci <- 400 >= ci_excess[1] & 400 <= ci_excess[2]
list(Proportion_Correct = is_in_prop_ci, ExcessPayment_Correct = is_in_excess_ci)
```
**Explanation**
Since 0.75 is not inside the CI from Part A, the estimate is likely overestimated.
Since 400 is inside the CI from Part B, the estimate is not overestimated.

## Problem 2 – Public vs Private

### Part A: Best test choice 
```{r}
filename <- "InsuranceClaims.csv"
InsuranceClaims <- read.csv(paste0(urlRemote, pathGithub, filename))
n <- nrow(InsuranceClaims)
x <- sum(InsuranceClaims$Buildup == 1)
p_hat <- x / n
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
z <- qnorm(0.975)
lower <- p_hat - z * se
upper <- p_hat + z * se
cat("Sample Proportion (p̂):", round(p_hat, 4), "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval for Population Proportion: [", round(lower, 4), ",", round(upper, 4), "]\n")
```
**Explanation**
To compare the means of two independent groups (Private vs. Public), use a two-sample t-test.

### Part B: Hypthothesis test 
```{r}
### Question 2B – Two-Sample t-Test to Compare Debt Levels

# Load data
urlRemote <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
pathGithub <- "EricBrownTTU/ISQS5346/main/"
filename <- "CollegeDebt.csv"
debt <- read.csv(paste0(urlRemote, pathGithub, filename))
t.test(debt[debt$Option == "Private",2],
       debt[debt$Option == "Public",2],
       alternative = "two.sided",
       var.equal = FALSE,
       conf.level = 0.95)
```
**Explanation** 
Since p < 0.05 (way smaller), you reject the null hypothesis.

## Problem 3 – Exit Survey
### Part A: Test of Independence
```{r}
urlRemote <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
pathGithub <- "EricBrownTTU/ISQS5346/main/"
filename <- "pgs.csv"
pgs <- read.csv(paste0(urlRemote, pathGithub, filename))

table_original <- table(pgs$FacTeaching, pgs$COL)
chisq.test(table_original)
```
**Explanation**
This test checks whether faculty teaching satisfaction and cost of living satisfaction are independent.

### Part B: Remove Sparse Column & Re-Test
```{r}
col_counts <- colSums(table_original)
min_col <- which.min(col_counts)
table_modified <- table_original[, -min_col]
chisq.test(table_modified)
```
**Explanation**
Removing sparse data can reduce noise and clarify relationships. Compare the p-value with that from part (a).
